findings.title: Inconsistent resource lookup key for all-clients permission check
findings.body: In hasPermission(String scope) the all-clients resource is looked up via resourceStore.findByName(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, server.getId()), while hasPermission(ClientModel, String) uses AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) to resolve the same 'all-clients' resource. Using two different lookup paths for what should be the same resource is fragile; if the resource type name differs from the resource name convention used elsewhere, this method will silently return false even when an all-clients permission exists, since it doesn't fall back to resolving via getResourceTypeResource like the other overload does.

findings.title: No fallback when resource.getScopes() doesn't include the needed scope semantics
findings.body: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), when the specific client resource exists, it is evaluated directly without checking whether an 'all-clients' permission could still grant extra permissions beyond what's modeled for the single resource (e.g. a MANAGE permission on all-clients should also grant VIEW/CONFIGURE even if the specific client resource only has a narrower permission). This differs from canManage()/canView() combos elsewhere that explicitly call multiple canX() methods for transitive scope checks, but hasPermission by itself does not combine both the specific-resource and all-resource evaluations, potentially under-granting access when both exist with different scopes.

findings.title: getClientsWithPermission returns resource names, not client IDs for 'all-clients' pseudo-resource
findings.body: getClientsWithPermission iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) and adds resource.getName() to the granted set. This will also include the pseudo resource named after CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE itself (the 'all-clients' resource), which is not an actual client ID. Callers treating the returned set as a list of real client IDs could get a bogus entry equal to the resource type name, causing invalid downstream behavior (e.g. attempting to look up a client with id 'Clients').
